The fixed asset note, movement by movement

Source: R/xbrl_movements.R
xbrl_movements.Rd

A filing's fixed asset schedule as it is printed: cost at the start of the year, the year's additions, disposals and transfers, cost at the end, then the same for accumulated depreciation and revaluation, and the carrying amount that falls out of them. One row per movement, per asset class, per filing.

Usage

xbrl_movements(
  x,
  category = c("tangible", "intangible"),
  basis = c("parent", "consolidated"),
  fill = TRUE
)

Arguments

x

A tibble from read_xbrl().

category

Which note: "tangible", "intangible", or both, which is the default. Financial assets are deliberately not here – buying shares in a subsidiary is not capital formation, and a note that swept them in would not be the fixed asset note.

basis

"parent" (default) or "consolidated". A group and its parent both report a fixed asset note, and the two sit next to each other undimensioned by class – without choosing, the same block comes back twice with different figures. An untagged figure is the parent's, because the taxonomy says so; see add_taxonomy().

fill

Derive a block the filer left out from the other two. FALSE returns only what was reported.

Value

A tibble in note order: the key – cvr, name, period_start, period_end – then what the row is (category, class, layer, item, label, elementid), what it says (value with the sign applied, tagged as the filer wrote it, currency, source), and how far to trust it (sign, sign_source, reconciled, covers_balance, covers_fixed_assets, continuous), with file last. A movement the filing does not report has no row.

Why long and not wide

The note is a roll-forward, and its point is that the arithmetic closes: opening plus additions less disposals equals closing, on each of three layers, and the three layers together give the carrying amount. A row per movement lets that be followed, checked, and filtered on. The note's own printed layout is one pivot_wider() away.

What the columns mean

layer is which of the note's blocks the row belongs to – "cost", "depreciation" (accumulated depreciation, amortisation and impairment), "revaluation", or "carrying" for the net figure the balance sheet carries. item is the row within the block: "opening" and "closing" for the balances, and "additions", "disposals", "transfers", "charge", "reversals" or "revaluations" for the movements between them. label is the two of them in Danish, as a printed note writes the line: "Kostpris primo", "Tilgang", "Årets af- og nedskrivninger".

The label is the package's own and not the taxonomy's, because the taxonomy's cannot name these rows. Opening and closing are the same element at two dates – PropertyPlantAndEquipmentGross is cost, and which balance it is depends on the instant it is tagged against – so the element's label names both and distinguishes neither. The filing's own declared period is what decides: period_end is the closing instant and the preceding period's end is the opening one. A row derived from the other two layers has no element at all, and is labelled just the same.

The signs are solved, and applied

A Danish filer tags a disposal as a positive number about as often as a negative one, so the figures as tagged do not roll forward. What decides the sign is the arithmetic: a layer closes for one assignment of plus and minus and not for the others, and there are few enough movements in a block to enumerate them.

value is the figure with that sign applied – a disposal is negative in it whatever the filer wrote – so a block sums: opening plus its movements is closing, and sum(value) over a company's additions is what it invested. tagged keeps the filer's own number beside it, NA on a derived row because no one tagged it.

sign_source says how the sign was arrived at, and the three answers are not equally strong:

  • "balance" – an opening or closing balance. A stated amount is not a movement and needs no sign; it is +1 and always was.

  • "solved" – the block's arithmetic closes for exactly this assignment.

  • "convention" – nothing could be solved, so the direction is taken from what the row is: a disposal or a reversal reduces its layer, everything else keeps the sign it was given. Checked against the rows where the arithmetic did settle it, the rule agrees 5,121 times out of 5,148.

Over the corpus that is 23,135 rows signed as balances, 5,148 solved and 498 by convention – and no row left without a figure to add up.

A caller who will only accept solved arithmetic filters on sign_source; one who wants the note as the filer wrote it reads tagged.

What is derived, and what is checked

source is "reported", "derived: layers", or "derived: first year" for the opening balance of a company that did not yet exist. The three blocks are a partition of one asset – carrying = cost - depreciation + revaluation at any instant – so a block the filer left out is determined by the other two. Over the whole corpus the identity closes to within a krone for 2,290 of the 2,358 blocks stating all three; read with depreciation added rather than subtracted it closes for 176. fill = FALSE returns only what was reported.

Four columns say whether to trust the result, and they answer different questions. A note can pass any one of them and fail another.

  • reconciled – does this block's roll-forward close within the year? Per filing, per class, per layer. NA where the filing gives no movements to check.

  • covers_balance – do the note's classes add up to the balance sheet line they belong to? A note covering land and buildings and stopping there is not wrong, but a figure taken from it is not the company's fixed assets. Over 4,304 filings, 1,378 class-broken notes cover their line and 99 do not. NA where the note has no class breakdown, because then the note's figure and the balance sheet's are the same fact and comparing them would be a tautology reported as a check.

  • covers_fixed_assets – do the two notes together account for the fixed assets the balance sheet carries? Per filing. A note can pass covers_balance and fail this: a filing that breaks down its tangible assets in full and says nothing about its intangibles is complete on the line it covers and silent on the rest. 1,198 filings pass and 109 fail; the remainder have no class-broken note to judge.

  • continuous – is the block's opening balance last year's closing balance? A schedule can close perfectly in every year and still break between them, when a company restates its cost or a filer starts the note over. The comparison is made on the opening row and the verdict is carried across the block, like the other three. Of 10,965 opening balances in the corpus, 7,387 had a preceding filing to compare with: 6,875 matched and 512 did not. NA where the company has no preceding filing in x – read one year and every row is NA, which is the commonest reason for seeing no TRUE at all.

The asset class

A note is tagged per class – land and buildings, plant and machinery, fixtures and fittings – with the total column often left untagged, because the balance sheet already carries it. class is the class where the filing tagged one and NA for the undimensioned figure. Summing across classes and the NA row counts everything twice.

How much of this a filing actually has

3,521 of 4,304 filings state a note at all, and most of them state very little of it. Counted by how many filings use each tangible-asset element: the carrying amount 3,471, cost 1,297, accumulated depreciation 1,181, the year's charge 1,120, additions 790, disposals 406, transfers 99. Intangible assets are a fraction of that again. The carrying amount and the charge are near-universal and the full schedule is a minority, so the rows simply do not appear where the filing is silent.

See also

xbrl_accounts(), which returns this beside the statements, check_movement() for the same reconciliation run over the raw facts, and find_signs() for the sign search on its own.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
x <- read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl")
m <- xbrl_movements(x)

# the note as it is printed
tidyr::pivot_wider(m, names_from = c(layer, item), values_from = value)

# what the companies invested in tangible assets, by year
a <- m[m$category == "tangible" & m$item == "additions", ]
tapply(a$value, format(a$period_end, "%Y"), sum)

# the same, on the schedules that close and nothing assumed
b <- a[a$reconciled %in% TRUE & a$sign_source == "solved", ]
} # }
